bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Project execution risk across 53 concurrent projects in challenging geographies — Geological uncertainty, adverse weather, equipment breakdown and unforeseen site conditions — particularly in high-altitude Himalayan and underground environments — can affect timelines, costs and delivery quality. Mitigation rests on 75+ years of complex project experience, dedicated on-site project management teams, contractual price escalation, force majeure and extension-of-time protections, and investment in advanced equipment.
- Order inflow lumpiness and concentration in a single government-funded segment — Dependence on government tendering cycles makes order inflows lumpy — FY25 inflows collapsed to Rs 1,112 million because of the election-year freeze — and over 62% of the order book is concentrated in hydropower, which is susceptible to policy and clearance delays. The Rs 1,51,193 million order book (2.96x book-to-bill), diversification across four verticals, spread over 14 states and 2 countries, and a near-term bidding pipeline of over Rs 6,00,000 million are the stated offsets, with FY26 inflow recovering to about Rs 44,000 million.
- Working-capital intensity and liquidity risk — Multi-year project timelines create billing-collection mismatches and potential liquidity pressure; adjusted net working capital stood at 106 days in FY26, within the stated 3-4 month normal operating range, with an initial mobilisation phase of 6-8 months typically preceding milestone-based billing. Mitigants cited are ~95% receivables collection efficiency, gross debt reduced to Rs 11,870 million, debt-to-equity at a five-year low of 0.27x, cash and equivalents of Rs 3,796 million, ~Rs 4,000 million of equity raised through the Rights Issue, the recently upgraded A (Stable) credit rating and diversified banking relationships.
- Commodity and input cost exposure under fixed-price contracts — EPC projects consume significant cement, steel, fuel and explosives, all exposed to global price volatility, and heightened Middle East conflict risk adds energy price uncertainty through FY27. Most projects carry contractual price escalation clauses allowing pass-through to clients, supported by prudent procurement and project-specific sourcing.
- Regulatory, environmental and clearance risk on hydropower and tunneling projects — Large projects in ecologically sensitive Himalayan and river-valley geographies require complex multi-stage statutory clearances, and mid-construction policy changes, forest rights issues or judicial intervention can stall projects and raise costs. Clearance risk sits primarily with the Government/PSU project developers (NHPC, SJVN, CVPPL) rather than with PEL as EPC contractor, and projects are increasingly awarded only after major clearances are in place.
- Geological and ground-condition risk in underground works — Actual ground conditions can differ from design assumptions, particularly in young Himalayan geology with complex faulting, high water inflows and squeezing rock; the Sleemanabad Carrier Canal's near two-decade construction history illustrates the extreme impact. Offsets cited are 300+ km of completed tunnels across NATM, TBM, EPB and hybrid mixed-face methods, state-of-the-art equipment including hybrid EPB machines and multi-mode TBMs, and an institutional knowledge base for adapting to adverse conditions.
- Competitive intensity in conventional civil infrastructure bidding — The infrastructure EPC sector is characterised by competitive bidding, particularly in irrigation and other conventional civil infrastructure projects, which may pressure order inflows and margins; the Company's defence is its strong position in specialised segments such as hydropower.
- Legacy non-core assets and stranded-investment risk — Land acquired in Tamil Nadu through subsidiaries for a proposed thermal power plant has been placed on hold with no active development, given India's shift toward renewable and storage-based generation, and the Company is evaluating options to monetise it. Hydropower development licenses held principally in Arunachal Pradesh are also under review pending evolving state policy conditions before the Company determines their future.
- Pending insolvency proceedings and the step into asset ownership — Three proceedings were pending before the NCLT Mumbai during FY 2025-26 against the Company under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, stated as pending for hearing and final disposal and as not materially impacting the business. Separately, the move from pure EPC into owning the 144 MW Gongri project on a BOOT basis under a 40-year concession introduces development and concession-asset exposure, with development activities expected to commence during the current financial year.

outlook.body:
- Four stated strategic priorities for the year: timely execution of the existing project portfolio, selective acquisition of quality orders, strengthening profitability and cash flows, and enhancing balance sheet efficiency
- Choose discipline over volume — prioritise margin-accretive, technically complex projects rather than chasing tender volume in an intensely competitive large-tender market
- Concentrate the portfolio in high-entry-barrier segments (hydropower, irrigation, tunneling) where engineering depth limits competition and protects margins
- Sustained deleveraging: reduce gross debt, improve the debt-to-equity ratio and repay the balance obligations including outstanding OCDs by FY 2027-28
- Monetise non-core assets on a recurring annual basis (land sales, arbitration recoveries) and use schemes such as Vivaad Se Vishwas, Niti Aayog guidelines for withdrawal of arbitration awards against bank guarantee and settlement of claims under CCI guidelines to accelerate monetisation of claims and variations, easing the working capital cycle
- Strategic evolution from builder to value creator — a deliberate step from pure EPC contracting toward owning long-life power-generation assets, beginning with the 144 MW Gongri Hydropower Project under a Build-Own-Operate model
- Selective international expansion — established presence in Nepal and Bhutan (Dorjilung project reinforcing the Bhutan presence), and evaluation of select Middle Eastern markets in reconstruction, water infrastructure, transportation and energy
- Build a more agile, technology-enabled and financially resilient organisation positioned where its engineering capabilities create the greatest competitive advantage, rather than simply executing more projects
- Continue investing in capability building, leadership development, safety excellence and digital skills for a future-ready workforce
- Reinvest profits in the business for future growth — no dividend recommended for FY2025-26

outlook.body: Patel Engineering is an EPC contractor, so its 'expansion' is expressed as project execution and order-book build-out rather than owned plant capacity, with one deliberate exception: a measured entry into asset ownership. The Company has entered into a Memorandum of Agreement with the Government of Arunachal Pradesh for the 144 MW Gongri Hydropower Project in West Kameng district on a BOOT basis with a 40-year concession; Dirang Energy Private Limited is the Special Purpose Company for the project, the GoAP has accorded in-principle approval for restoration of the project, the MOA is dated 18th December 2025, and DPR approval and TEV study work has been initiated. On the execution side, FY26 highlights include the Subansiri Lower HEP (2,000 MW, client NHPC, on the bordering districts of Assam and Arunachal Pradesh), where structural civil works are fully completed for 6 of 8 powerhouse units, 4 of 8 generating units are commissioned, mass concreting exceeding 6.5 lakh cubic meters has been executed, and ongoing activity is finalising the machine halls for Units 7 and 8, architectural finishes, electro-mechanical integration, concrete lining and grouting of the remaining surge tunnel access, and the final phases of remaining underground excavation; Units 5 through 8 are in advanced stages of construction and scheduled to be commissioned in phases by the end of the year. Other projects under execution include Kiru HEP (624 MW, J&K, client CVPPL) with over 11,50,000 cubic meters of dam concreting completed and powerhouse units 1-3 completed; Kwar HEP (540 MW, J&K, client CVPPL) with over 3,00,000 cubic meters of dam concreting and breakthroughs at the Main Access Tunnel, Dam Top Road Tunnel, Pressure Shaft 4 and Surge Gallery 2; Parnai HEP (37.5 MW, J&K, client JKSPDC) with HRT intake, barrage and desilting basin structures completed; Arun III (900 MW, Nepal, client SAPDC) with Units 1-3 machine hall slab, head race tunnel and surge shaft lining completed; Kundah Pumped Storage Project (500 MW, Tamil Nadu, client Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation Ltd) with a 969.11 meter tail race tunnel breakthrough, powerhouse and surge chamber civil works and upper intake structure completed; Teesta VI HEP (500 MW, Sikkim, client NHPC); Shongtong HEP (450 MW, Himachal Pradesh, client HPPCL) with over 2,50,000 cubic meters of dam concreting completed out of a total 4,00,000 cubic meters and all civil works for the 3 powerhouse units completed; Tunnel T-7 (3.08 km, West Bengal & Sikkim, client Ircon International Ltd); the CIDCO Treated Water Tunnel - II Project (6.2 km, Maharashtra), completed more than 3 months ahead of schedule with a national record of 812 meters of TBM tunneling in a single month in January 2026; the Sleemanabad Irrigation Project (12 km tunnel, Madhya Pradesh) with 11.7 km of tunneling completed and breakthrough achieved post year end; and the Rihand Micro Irrigation Project (38,000 Ha culturable command area, Madhya Pradesh). The forward opportunity set the Company points to includes a near-term large-hydro tendering pipeline of over 11,000 MW (Upper Karnali 900 MW, Kalai-II 1,200 MW, Kamala 1,720 MW, Sawalkote 1,856 MW, Subansiri Upper ~1,600 MW, Kirthai-II 820 MW and Etalin 3,097 MW), a J&K acceleration following the April 2025 suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty, Arunachal Pradesh's declared 2025-35 'Decade of Hydropower', and the CEA's 100 GW pumped storage target for 2035-36.

outlook.body:
- Energy transition super cycle creates enduring demand for hydropower and pumped storage construction, segments in which PEL holds a leadership position in India; over 50 GW of identified hydropower and pumped storage development potential and a national pumped storage target of 100 GW by 2035-36
- Global premium on energy security, heightened by Middle East conflict risk, reinforces political commitment across South and Southeast Asia to accelerate domestic energy capacity addition — giving policy support behind Indian infrastructure investment a structural durability that transcends any individual budget cycle
- Untapped hydropower potential in Nepal and Bhutan; Bhutan's hydropower expansion programme presents a compelling long-term opportunity
- Union Budget FY2026-27 raised public capital expenditure to Rs 12.2 trillion (approximately 3.1% of GDP), an 11.5% increase over the FY26 revised estimate, extending a six-fold rise over a decade; effective capital expenditure reaches Rs 17.15 trillion
- Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund announced in the Budget provides partial credit guarantees to private infrastructure developers, expected to increase project viability and accelerate tendering across hydropower, tunneling and urban water infrastructure
- Seven announced High-Speed Rail Corridors, and high-speed rail investments exceeding Rs 1.2 trillion, will require extensive tunneling and civil engineering works
- Metro and RRTS programmes — 38 metro rail projects sanctioned covering 1,051 km at an estimated cost of Rs 3.44 trillion, Rs 80,000 Mn allocated for RRTS expansion and Rs 22,000 Mn granted to the National Capital Region Transport Corporation — represent a growing pipeline of tunneling-intensive civil construction
- Jal Jeevan Mission extended to December 2028 with around Rs 6,76,700 Mn allocated toward water supply and irrigation projects
- Around 30 planned river-linking projects at an estimated cost of nearly Rs 8 trillion are expected to create large-scale irrigation and water transfer opportunities aligned to the Company's strengths in the medium term
- Ministry of New and Renewable Energy allocation raised to Rs 3,29,140 Mn from Rs 2,65,490 Mn in FY26, and restructuring of PFC and REC as long-term infrastructure financiers, improving bankability of complex hydropower and energy storage projects
- Indian macro backdrop: real GDP grew 7.7% in FY2025-26 (from 7.1% in FY2024-25) with Gross Fixed Capital Formation up 8.2%; Economic Survey 2025-26 projects FY27 real GDP growth of 6.8% to 7.2%
- Global economy expected to expand at a moderate pace with growth revised down to 3.1% for 2026 amid the Middle East conflict; cumulative global infrastructure investment of US$151.1 trillion forecast over 2024-2050, reinforcing the value of specialised hydropower, water, tunneling and climate-resilient capabilities
- Margin lever: profitability improved even as the top line held steady, reflecting a leaner cost structure and a materially lower interest burden, with finance costs down 8.1%; credit rating improvement from BBB- to A (Stable) lowers the cost of borrowing
- Revenue mix anchored in high-entry-barrier segments — Hydropower 55%, Irrigation 23%, Tunneling 17% and Roads, Urban Infrastructure & Others 5% of full-year revenue
- Order book of Rs 1,51,193 million as of March 31, 2026, across 53 ongoing projects spread across 14 states domestically plus international presence in Nepal and Bhutan — a Book-to-Bill ratio of 2.96x, underwriting roughly three years of revenue visibility
- FY26 order inflows of Rs 44,009 million, a dramatic recovery from the Rs 1,112 million recorded in FY25, which was heavily impacted by the general elections
- FY26 order intake diversified across hydropower (47.5%), urban infrastructure (30%), irrigation (4.4%) and others (18.1%)
- Year-end order book composition reflects core strengths: hydropower 62.7%, irrigation 16.2%, urban infrastructure and others 15.0%, tunneling 4.8% and roads 1.3%
- Over 92% of the order book is from Central Government / PSU and State Government clients, providing high payment security
- New orders won during FY26 include the Kondhane Dam (~Rs 13,000 Mn), Renuka Ji Dam (~Rs 9,000 Mn), HEO Hydropower (~Rs 7,000 Mn), the Dorjilung Hydropower Project (~Rs 2,300 Mn) in Bhutan, Teesta V Power Station (~Rs 2,400 Mn) in Sikkim and coal-mining packages (~Rs 8,000 Mn) in Madhya Pradesh

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Patel Engineering is an Indian civil-construction and EPC contractor with an undisputed leadership position in India's hydropower and tunneling sectors, having completed more than 350 projects.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Patel Engineering delivers integrated civil construction solutions for large-scale infrastructure — hydropower projects (surface, underground and sub-surface powerhouses, intake structures, penstocks, pressure shafts, tunnels, switchyards and access systems), road, rail and water-conveyance tunnels, dams, canals, lift irrigation and pipe distribution networks, and transport and urban infrastructure. Its clients are predominantly Central Government departments and PSUs and State Governments, with a smaller international presence in Nepal and Bhutan. Multidisciplinary teams of engineers, geologists and project specialists, supported by a network of partners and subcontractors, execute technically complex work in geologically challenging Himalayan and sub-Himalayan terrain.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Energy transition super cycle creates enduring demand for hydropower and pumped storage construction, segments in which PEL holds a leadership position in India; over 50 GW of identified hydropower and pumped storage development potential and a national pumped storage target of 100 GW by 2035-36
- Global premium on energy security, heightened by Middle East conflict risk, reinforces political commitment across South and Southeast Asia to accelerate domestic energy capacity addition — giving policy support behind Indian infrastructure investment a structural durability that transcends any individual budget cycle
- Untapped hydropower potential in Nepal and Bhutan; Bhutan's hydropower expansion programme presents a compelling long-term opportunity
- Union Budget FY2026-27 raised public capital expenditure to Rs 12.2 trillion (approximately 3.1% of GDP), an 11.5% increase over the FY26 revised estimate, extending a six-fold rise over a decade; effective capital expenditure reaches Rs 17.15 trillion
- Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund announced in the Budget provides partial credit guarantees to private infrastructure developers, expected to increase project viability and accelerate tendering across hydropower, tunneling and urban water infrastructure
- Seven announced High-Speed Rail Corridors, and high-speed rail investments exceeding Rs 1.2 trillion, will require extensive tunneling and civil engineering works
- Metro and RRTS programmes — 38 metro rail projects sanctioned covering 1,051 km at an estimated cost of Rs 3.44 trillion, Rs 80,000 Mn allocated for RRTS expansion and Rs 22,000 Mn granted to the National Capital Region Transport Corporation — represent a growing pipeline of tunneling-intensive civil construction
- Jal Jeevan Mission extended to December 2028 with around Rs 6,76,700 Mn allocated toward water supply and irrigation projects
- Around 30 planned river-linking projects at an estimated cost of nearly Rs 8 trillion are expected to create large-scale irrigation and water transfer opportunities aligned to the Company's strengths in the medium term
- Ministry of New and Renewable Energy allocation raised to Rs 3,29,140 Mn from Rs 2,65,490 Mn in FY26, and restructuring of PFC and REC as long-term infrastructure financiers, improving bankability of complex hydropower and energy storage projects
- Indian macro backdrop: real GDP grew 7.7% in FY2025-26 (from 7.1% in FY2024-25) with Gross Fixed Capital Formation up 8.2%; Economic Survey 2025-26 projects FY27 real GDP growth of 6.8% to 7.2%
- Global economy expected to expand at a moderate pace with growth revised down to 3.1% for 2026 amid the Middle East conflict; cumulative global infrastructure investment of US$151.1 trillion forecast over 2024-2050, reinforcing the value of specialised hydropower, water, tunneling and climate-resilient capabilities
- Margin lever: profitability improved even as the top line held steady, reflecting a leaner cost structure and a materially lower interest burden, with finance costs down 8.1%; credit rating improvement from BBB- to A (Stable) lowers the cost of borrowing
- Revenue mix anchored in high-entry-barrier segments — Hydropower 55%, Irrigation 23%, Tunneling 17% and Roads, Urban Infrastructure & Others 5% of full-year revenue
- Order book of Rs 1,51,193 million as of March 31, 2026, across 53 ongoing projects spread across 14 states domestically plus international presence in Nepal and Bhutan — a Book-to-Bill ratio of 2.96x, underwriting roughly three years of revenue visibility
- FY26 order inflows of Rs 44,009 million, a dramatic recovery from the Rs 1,112 million recorded in FY25, which was heavily impacted by the general elections
- FY26 order intake diversified across hydropower (47.5%), urban infrastructure (30%), irrigation (4.4%) and others (18.1%)
- Year-end order book composition reflects core strengths: hydropower 62.7%, irrigation 16.2%, urban infrastructure and others 15.0%, tunneling 4.8% and roads 1.3%
- Over 92% of the order book is from Central Government / PSU and State Government clients, providing high payment security
- New orders won during FY26 include the Kondhane Dam (~Rs 13,000 Mn), Renuka Ji Dam (~Rs 9,000 Mn), HEO Hydropower (~Rs 7,000 Mn), the Dorjilung Hydropower Project (~Rs 2,300 Mn) in Bhutan, Teesta V Power Station (~Rs 2,400 Mn) in Sikkim and coal-mining packages (~Rs 8,000 Mn) in Madhya Pradesh

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Patel Engineering is an EPC contractor, so its 'expansion' is expressed as project execution and order-book build-out rather than owned plant capacity, with one deliberate exception: a measured entry into asset ownership. The Company has entered into a Memorandum of Agreement with the Government of Arunachal Pradesh for the 144 MW Gongri Hydropower Project in West Kameng district on a BOOT basis with a 40-year concession; Dirang Energy Private Limited is the Special Purpose Company for the project, the GoAP has accorded in-principle approval for restoration of the project, the MOA is dated 18th December 2025, and DPR approval and TEV study work has been initiated. On the execution side, FY26 highlights include the Subansiri Lower HEP (2,000 MW, client NHPC, on the bordering districts of Assam and Arunachal Pradesh), where structural civil works are fully completed for 6 of 8 powerhouse units, 4 of 8 generating units are commissioned, mass concreting exceeding 6.5 lakh cubic meters has been executed, and ongoing activity is finalising the machine halls for Units 7 and 8, architectural finishes, electro-mechanical integration, concrete lining and grouting of the remaining surge tunnel access, and the final phases of remaining underground excavation; Units 5 through 8 are in advanced stages of construction and scheduled to be commissioned in phases by the end of the year. Other projects under execution include Kiru HEP (624 MW, J&K, client CVPPL) with over 11,50,000 cubic meters of dam concreting completed and powerhouse units 1-3 completed; Kwar HEP (540 MW, J&K, client CVPPL) with over 3,00,000 cubic meters of dam concreting and breakthroughs at the Main Access Tunnel, Dam Top Road Tunnel, Pressure Shaft 4 and Surge Gallery 2; Parnai HEP (37.5 MW, J&K, client JKSPDC) with HRT intake, barrage and desilting basin structures completed; Arun III (900 MW, Nepal, client SAPDC) with Units 1-3 machine hall slab, head race tunnel and surge shaft lining completed; Kundah Pumped Storage Project (500 MW, Tamil Nadu, client Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation Ltd) with a 969.11 meter tail race tunnel breakthrough, powerhouse and surge chamber civil works and upper intake structure completed; Teesta VI HEP (500 MW, Sikkim, client NHPC); Shongtong HEP (450 MW, Himachal Pradesh, client HPPCL) with over 2,50,000 cubic meters of dam concreting completed out of a total 4,00,000 cubic meters and all civil works for the 3 powerhouse units completed; Tunnel T-7 (3.08 km, West Bengal & Sikkim, client Ircon International Ltd); the CIDCO Treated Water Tunnel - II Project (6.2 km, Maharashtra), completed more than 3 months ahead of schedule with a national record of 812 meters of TBM tunneling in a single month in January 2026; the Sleemanabad Irrigation Project (12 km tunnel, Madhya Pradesh) with 11.7 km of tunneling completed and breakthrough achieved post year end; and the Rihand Micro Irrigation Project (38,000 Ha culturable command area, Madhya Pradesh). The forward opportunity set the Company points to includes a near-term large-hydro tendering pipeline of over 11,000 MW (Upper Karnali 900 MW, Kalai-II 1,200 MW, Kamala 1,720 MW, Sawalkote 1,856 MW, Subansiri Upper ~1,600 MW, Kirthai-II 820 MW and Etalin 3,097 MW), a J&K acceleration following the April 2025 suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty, Arunachal Pradesh's declared 2025-35 'Decade of Hydropower', and the CEA's 100 GW pumped storage target for 2035-36.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Undisputed leadership position in India's hydropower sector, with capabilities spanning projects from 3 MW to over 2,800 MW across India and neighbouring countries
- Seven-decade track record and more than 350 completed projects, including 87+ dams, 300+ km of tunnels and involvement in the civil construction of 15,000+ MW of hydro capacity
- Proven execution in geologically challenging Himalayan and sub-Himalayan terrain — a barrier that narrows the pool of credible bidders and supports pricing discipline
- Advanced tunneling technology base (TBM, NATM, drill-and-blast), evidenced by a national record of 812 meters of TBM tunneling in a single month at CIDCO TWT-II
- Engineering firsts that serve as reference credentials: Asia's first underwater double lake tapping at Koyna HEP, India's first piano key weir at Sawrakuddu HEP, first Indian company to execute a micro-tunneling and HDD project for urban water infrastructure at the MCGM Water Supply Project, and the world's longest bi-lane road tunnel at Sela Pass
- Deep, repeat client relationships — participation at multiple nodes of the same integrated water supply system at CIDCO (TWT-II plus the Kondhane Dam award)
- Deliberate portfolio concentration in high-entry-barrier segments (hydropower, tunneling, irrigation), where engineering depth limits competition and protects margins
- Materially strengthened balance sheet — gross debt at its lowest level in a decade and a credit rating that has climbed from BBB- to A (Stable), enabling larger bids
